report:
Your “yes” is too broad: for typical knee osteoarthritis pain, arthroscopy/lavage/debridement does **not** show meaningful benefit. The key sham-controlled trial found arthroscopic lavage/debridement no better than placebo, and the Cochrane review concluded there is “gold” level evidence that debridement has no benefit for undiscriminated knee OA: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18254069/

Major guidelines align with that. AAOS recommends against arthroscopy with lavage and/or debridement for a primary diagnosis of knee OA: https://www.aaos.org/globalassets/quality-and-practice-resources/osteoarthritis-of-the-knee/oak3cpg.pdf . A BMJ/BJSM clinical practice guideline strongly recommends against arthroscopic surgery for most degenerative knee disease: https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/52/5/313 .

Important exception: true mechanical locking (not stiffness or “giving way”) may justify referral; UK evidence-based commissioning says arthroscopy should not be offered for OA unless there is a clear locking history: https://ebi.aomrc.org.uk/interventions/knee-arthroscopy-for-patients-with-osteoarthritis/ .

So the evidence supports “no” for routine knee OA symptoms, with a narrow mechanical-locking caveat. First-line care is exercise/physiotherapy, weight management if relevant, analgesia, and consideration of injections or joint replacement when appropriate.
